title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
This week, I set up the basic workflow for my course portfolio. I created a repository from the course template, cloned it to my computer with GitHub Desktop, opened the project in RStudio, edited a Quarto file, and rendered it as a webpage. I then committed and pushed the changes to GitHub so that they could appear on my GitHub Pages site.
I also learned that a website can be understood as a collection of HTML files stored on a computer or server. Quarto helps create those HTML files: I write content in a .qmd file, and Quarto renders it into an .html file that a web browser can display.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.






TipDelete this box

In this analysis, I look at [YOUR VARIABLE] across counties in [YOUR STATE], and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 06001 Alameda County, California     38.7    0.2 1651949    NA
2 06003 Alpine County, California      41.1    4.8    1695   234
3 06005 Amador County, California      49.9    0.6   41029    NA
4 06007 Butte County, California       36.3    0.2  209470    NA
5 06009 Calaveras County, California   52      0.7   45995    NA
6 06011 Colusa County, California      35.7    0.9   21895    NA








NoteDelete this box



Notice the column names: myvarE, myvarM, popE, popM. The E and M suffixes are estimate and margin of error.



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         56        700685.
2 Moderate                 2          2213 








NoteDelete this box



Two blanks. What are you grouping by? What are you averaging? :::grouping by reliability, and average the estimate population






TipDelete this box



This table is the heart of the assignment. Describe what it shows in two or three sentences.


[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?]
— The average population of high-confidence counties is 700,685 versus 2,213 for the low-confidence counties. Fewer population will bring lower confidence.

Optional challenges - For those craving more






NoteDelete this box



None of these are graded. There are no extra points. A complete, well-written assignment earns a 2 either way.
They’re here for anyone who finished the above and found it straightforward. Pick one (or more) that interests you.

Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.
Parameterize the report. Add params: to the YAML so the state is an input rather than hard-coded, and the same file regenerates for any state. Render it from the terminal with quarto render assignment2.qmd -P state:NY.
Write a function and iterate. Wrap the data pull in a function, then use purrr::map_dfr() to run it across several states at once. Does the small-places-are-noisier pattern hold everywhere, or are some states different?
Change the geographic scale. Run the same variable at geography = "tract" inside one county. Compare the margins of error to what you saw at county level. What does that imply about the resolution at which you can actually trust ACS data?

If you try one, add a short section describing what you did and what you found.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
[Your 200–250 word reflection goes here.]
Among California counties, Alpine and Sierra have the greatest relative uncertainty in their median age estimates. Alpine County has an estimated median age of 41.1 years and a margin of error (MoE) of 4.8 years (11.68% of the estimate). Sierra County has an estimated median age of 56 years and a MoE of 5 years (8.93%). Both are measured less precisely than other counties.
Using relative MOE cutoffs of 0.5% and 1%, the 16 high-confidence counties average roughly 1,711,758 residents, compared with 25,185 for the 16 low-confidence counties. The 26 moderate-confidence counties average 440,450. This pattern reflects how the ACS works: it surveys a sample of residents, and smaller counties yield fewer observations, so their estimates carry more uncertainty.
Suppose a state agency used median age to prioritize funding for older-adult services. An underestimated median age might cause a county to miss support; an overestimate might divert funding from communities that need it. Alpine and Sierra would be especially exposed to such errors. Agencies should weigh MoE alongside point estimates — and recognize that median age alone does not capture the number of older residents who need services.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Optional challenges - For those craving more
text:
Optional challenges - For those craving more
Using 2023 ACS five-year estimates, I compared the precision of median age estimates for Los Angeles County and its census tracts. The county’s relative MOE was 0.26%, while the median relative MOE across 2,477 valid tracts was 10.12%. Another 21 tracts were excluded for missing estimates.
With reliability thresholds at 5% and 10%, 181 tracts (7.31%) fell into high confidence, 1,037 (41.87%) into moderate, and 1,259 (50.83%) into low confidence.
A precise county estimate does not guarantee equally precise estimates at the tract level. Smaller areas yield fewer survey observations and more uncertainty. Agencies directing older-adult services to specific neighborhoods should check tract-level MOEs rather than relying on county precision alone.

title: Week 3: Visulaization
text:
Key Concepts

Anscombe’s Quartet
The four datasets have the same or nearly identical mean x, mean y, correlation, and regression line, but very different distributions when plotted.


How to Build a ggplot

Step 1: Assign an object and create a blank canvas
p <- ggplot(data)

# You can also start without specifying data
p <- ggplot()


Step 2: Define aesthetic mappings
aes() maps data to visual properties such as position and color.

Inside aes(): map a variable or category to a visual property.
Outside aes(): set a visual property to a fixed value.

# Map the category "blue" to color.
# This creates a legend labeled "blue";
# it does not necessarily make the points blue.
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct, color = "blue") +
  geom_point()

# Set all points to blue
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")

# Color points according to the city variable
ggplot(df, aes(x = income, y = rent)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = city))


Step 3: Choose a geometry



Function
Purpose




geom_histogram()
Show the distribution of a variable


geom_point()
Show the relationship between two variables


geom_boxplot()
Compare distributions across groups


geom_col()
Compare values across groups


geom_line()
Show changes over time


geom_errorbar()
Display uncertainty



p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = income, y = rent, color = city)) +
  geom_point()
The + operator adds layers or other plot components.



ACS Error and Reliability

Standard Error (SE)
For an ACS margin of error reported at the 90% confidence level:
\[
SE = \frac{MOE}{1.645}
\]


Coefficient of Variation (CV)
\[
CV = \frac{SE}{\text{Estimate}} \times 100%
\]
CV thresholds from the class notes:



CV Level
Range
Interpretation




Low
< 15%
High reliability


Medium
15%–30%



High
> 30%
High sampling error





Uncertainty in Derived Estimates
When calculating sums, proportions, or ratios, account for uncertainty in the original estimates. Both the numerator and denominator may have sampling error.








Function
Purpose
Example




moe_sum()
Calculate the MOE of a sum
Add populations across several areas


moe_prop()
Calculate the MOE of a part-to-whole proportion
Population in poverty ÷ population for whom poverty status is determined


moe_ratio()
Calculate the MOE of a general ratio
Number of jobs ÷ number of housing units





Changes Over Time
When comparing ACS multiyear estimates, use periods with non-overlapping years.
Convert each period’s MOE to its standard error:
\[
SE_1 = \frac{MOE_1}{1.645},
\qquad
SE_2 = \frac{MOE_2}{1.645}
\]
Assuming the two estimates are independent, the standard error of the difference is:
\[
SE_{\text{diff}} = \sqrt{SE_1^2 + SE_2^2}
\]
Define the difference as:
\[
\text{Difference} = \text{Estimate}_1 - \text{Estimate}_2
\]
The Z-score is:
\[
Z = \frac{\text{Estimate}_1 - \text{Estimate}2}{SE{\text{diff}}}
\]
The 90% confidence interval for the change is:
\[
\text{Difference} \pm 1.645 \times SE_{\text{diff}}
\]
